evidence.excerpt:
Many long-term memory systems for LLM agents are built around embedding-based retrieval. Al-
though effective for semantic matching, similarity ranking alone does not establish whether re-
trieved memories satisfy the conditions implied by a question. In this paper, we introduce KITE
(Knowledge-IndexedTemporalEvidence), a vector-free framework that formulates memory re-
trieval as an explicit decision procedure. KITE organizes multi-session conversations as structured
knowledge indexed by a governed topic vocabulary, which evolves through controlled expansion
and consolidation. At query time, questions are compiled into inspectable retrieval plans over the
same knowledge index that guides memory construction. The plans are then executed through fixed
lookup and ranking operations, while sparse lexical retrieval recovers surface details omitted from
the structured representation.

Governed topic vocabulary.Rather than assuming a complete ontology in advance, KITE derives its topic vocab-
ulary from the accumulated conversation history. Starting from a small set of canonical roots, the extraction model
reuses existing topics when possible and gradually proposes more specific children when new concepts emerge. To
ensure consistency, new topics must fit within the existing hierarchy, which helps maintain a stable index over time.

each question is interpreted against the stored vocabulary and entities. Thus, references inferred from the question can
be resolved to existing index keys, keeping query interpretation aligned with memory organization. The compiler then
maps the question to these keys, while the executor determines which memories satisfy the resulting conditions.

Subqueries can be linked sequentially, allowing results from an earlier step to constrain the search performed in

Plan validation.Before execution, each plan is validated against a fixed typed grammar and the knowledge index.
Indexed references are resolved to valid keys in the governed representation. Speaker mentions are mapped to par-
ticipant constraints, while temporal expressions are normalized into explicit ranges. Plans with unresolved references
or unsupported structures are rejected. The validated plan is executed by the retrieval executor without further model
intervention, drawing a clear boundary between model-based interpretation and deterministic evidence selection.

2024) and LongMemEval-S (Wu et al., 2025). Specifically, the LoCoMo experiments cover 1,540 questions across

Benchmarks.We evaluate KITE on two long-term conversational memory benchmarks, LoCoMo (Maharana et al.,
2024) and LongMemEval-S (Wu et al., 2025). Specifically, the LoCoMo experiments cover 1,540 questions across
ten multi-session conversations, while LongMemEval-S comprises 500 questions over longer interaction histories.

mussen et al., 2025), MemOS (Li et al., 2025), and EverMemOS (Hu et al., 2026a). We also consider Naive RAG as
a retrieval baseline and full-context inference over the complete conversation history as a non-retrieval reference.

Superior vector-free performance.Tables 1 and 2 show that KITE achieves the highest overall accuracy among
the compared systems without relying on dense embeddings or neural reranking. It reaches an accuracy of 93.5%
on LoCoMo, outperforming EverMemOS by 0.4 percentage points, and 86.0% on the LongMemEval-S questions,
widening the margin to 3.0 percentage points. Compared with full-context inference, KITE further improves accuracy
by 2.6 and 29.2 percentage points on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, respectively. Overall, these results show that
strong long-term memory performance does not require dense similarity retrieval or full-history input to the reader.

ing, where it achieves 92.2% on LoCoMo and 85.7% on LongMemEval-S, with the latter exceeding the next-best result

To isolate the effect of retrieval from memory construction, we freeze the memory store and compare retrieval strate-
gies over the same representations. We compare dense-vector retrieval, BM25, and their hybrid with KITE's plan-
guided retrieval. For a controlled comparison, all methods share identical reader settings and reader-context token
budgets, with LLM-as-a-judge accuracy and evidence recall measuring answer quality and retrieval effectiveness.
Table 3 shows that KITE achieves the highest accuracy and recall on both benchmarks with memory construction held
fixed. Notably, recall is consistently lower than accuracy on LoCoMo because the gold evidence often includes more
dialogue turns than are strictly necessary to answer the question. A correct answer may therefore be produced without
retrieving every annotated turn. Even so, KITE improves recall over the hybrid baseline by 7.5

and time periods, while KITE further consolidates redundant sibling topics. Each variant uses its resulting topic

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Evidence recall is computed against benchmark-annotated gold evidence units, independent of the LLM judge, and moves in the same direction as accuracy across retrieval-strategy comparisons.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Headline outcomes are LLM-as-a-judge accuracy using gpt-4.1-mini as judge, supplemented by objective evidence recall against annotated gold dialogue turns and sessions.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: The system's design choices—topic governance rules, extraction prompts, query compilation prompts, fixed scoring weights, and reciprocal rank fusion—are hand-designed and not tuned against the reported accuracy metric.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding superior temporal and multi-hop reasoning, compact reader context sizes (1.5k–1.6k tokens), and strong performance without dense embeddings are well supported by quantitative benchmark and ablation tables.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation is conducted across two recognized benchmarks (LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S) comparing against competitive persistent memory baselines, dense retrieval, and full-context models using both LLM-as-a-judge accuracy and objective ground-truth evidence recall. In addition, extensive ablations clearly isolate the contributions of faceted indexing, deterministic ranking, topic governance, and dual retrieval paths.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Objective evidence recall computed against annotated gold dialogue turns (LoCoMo) and gold sessions (LongMemEval-S).
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: LLM-as-a-judge accuracy evaluating answer correctness along with objective ground-truth evidence recall across annotated conversation turns/sessions.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: System rules, prompt engineering, and heuristic rank-fusion parameters designed for memory extraction and query plan execution.

primary.limitations: The authors transparently report that the method underperforms on single-session preference queries (63.3% on LongMemEval-S) due to difficulties in capturing indirect or paraphrased preference expressions into the structured index.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, specifying structured extraction schemas, governance rules for vocabulary expansion and consolidation, index structures, query compilation grammar, and deterministic plan execution with rule-based scoring and reciprocal rank fusion.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents an inventive, non-circular, vector-free approach to conversational memory retrieval, thoroughly describes system components and prompts, and validates design choices through standard benchmarks, objective recall metrics, and well-designed ablation experiments.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces KITE, a vector-free conversational memory framework that organizes multi-session dialogue into structured, faceted facts under an evolving topic vocabulary and evaluates retrieval as an explicit, plan-compiled decision procedure executed over index postings alongside sparse lexical search.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents an inventive, non-circular, vector-free approach to conversational memory retrieval, thoroughly describes system components and prompts, and validates design choices through standard benchmarks, objective recall metrics, and well-designed ablation experiments.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors transparently report that the method underperforms on single-session preference queries (63.3% on LongMemEval-S) due to difficulties in capturing indirect or paraphrased preference expressions into the structured index.
